findings.claim: The cap check compares each refund against the full payment amount and never subtracts what was already refunded (store.refundedFor exists but is unused), so a payment of 100 can be refunded 60 + 60 = 120, exceeding the payment. The API documents a refund as at most what is left, answered with 422.

proof.Reason: the test failed in two separate runs on the PR head and passes on the fixed tree

findings.claim: getRefund only checks that some X-Merchant-ID header is present and then returns any refund by id, so merchant m-2 can read m-1's refund (200 with full payment/merchant/amount data). GET /refunds/{id} documents 404 and the service's own convention is to hide other merchants' objects; the calling merchant must be compared with ref.MerchantID (and Service.Get must enforce it).

proof.Reason: the test failed in two separate runs on the PR head and passes on the fixed tree

findings.claim: The middleware only sets the header on the response; it never puts the id into the request context nor into the caller's header, so handlers/components that need to correlate their logs with the request id cannot read it. The new tests are wired to avoid that (they only inspect the recorder header). Consumers of app.New get requests whose r.Context() carries no request id, so the stated purpose (tying a request to its log lines) is not served.

proof.Reason: the test did not build on the PR head, and a build error is not a fail

findings.claim: The caller-supplied X-Request-ID is echoed verbatim without any validation or sanitisation, so an attacker can inject arbitrary content (e.g. CR/LF-ish or extremely long values, or values designed to poison downstream log parsing) into the response header and into any log line that carries it. A request id should be length-limited and character-restricted, and replaced by a generated id when it does not match.

proof.Reason: the test did not build on the fixed tree, and a build error is not a pass

findings.claim: The generated id counter lives inside the middleware closure while the package also has its own independent id scheme; more importantly the middleware generates ids only from a process-local counter that restarts at req_1, so ids collide across restarts and across multiple app instances built in the same or different processes, defeating the stated purpose of tying a request to its log lines across a fleet.

proof.Reason: the test did not build on the fixed tree, and a build error is not a pass
